chunks: A number of our companions, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Khalid, from Uthman ibn Isa, from Sama'ah ibn Mihran, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said:
Whoever seizes a thief and pardons him, that is up to him; but if it is raised to the Imam, he cuts him.
So if the one from whom it was stolen says, 'I gift it to him,' the Imam will not leave him until he cuts him, when it is raised to him.
And indeed, the gifting is before it is raised to the Imam.
And the preservers of the Penalties of Allah
So when the Penalty ends up with the Imam, it is not for anyone that he should leave it.

key_terms.الحافظون لحدود الله: The preservers of the Penalties of Allah

ai.seo_question: What is the difference between a victim's pardon and the Imam's enforcement of the theft penalty in Shia fiqh?
ai.summary: This hadith clarifies the jurisprudential distinction between the victim's private right to pardon (afw) and the public right of the Imam (haqq al-imam) in theft cases, a key concept in Shia fiqh. It establishes that while the victim can waive their share before the case is formally elevated to the Imam, the divine limit (hadd) becomes obligatory upon the Imam's authority, rendering subsequent gifts ineffective. This ruling underscores the principle that hadd punishments are ultimately acts of divine justice rather than mere private compensation.
